rv.q: There’s not one false note in director Daniel Sullivan’s clear direction or in the natural yet precise performances of Linney and Hecht, who are working at the top of their game and together offer a master class in acting.
Loved this play – exquisitely acted, sublime, subtle and impactful in its universal relatability.
They are a gorgeous duo, these friends: bickering lifelines for each other, vulnerable and too proud.
The closer you look, and listen, and the more you reflect upon it, the deeper grow its rewards.
In a way, the story's modesty allows emotion and meaning to suddenly sneak up on you.
The key pleasure of Summer, 1976 comes from listening to Laura Linney and Jessica Hecht talk.
It’s a dramatic dream team; what’s missing is drama.
Because of that, Summer, 1976 is a must-see–a rare perfect play with two brilliant performances at the center.

A world premiere production of the Manhattan Theatre Club at the Samuel J. Friedman Theatre, Summer, 1976 has been directed by Daniel Sullivan whose nuanced approach turns Auburn’s words into three-dimensional portraits.
His coordination of the technical elements is equally arresting.
Instead, Summer, 1976 highlights how simpler moments and interactions along one's timeline can still have a profound and long-lasting impact — much like the play itself.
It's a measure of the care with which Summer, 1976 has been written, produced, and performed that, days later, you may find yourself musing about Diana and Alice.
Director Daniel Sullivan deftly delineates every interaction – subdued to explosive.
In fact, if this accessible and often charming play won’t earn Mr. Auburn another Pulitzer, I can easily picture it enduring as a showcase for any number of gifted actresses.

Linney and Hecht are excellent and generous scene partners, and though Summer, 1976 has none of the explosive bells and whistles of some of its Broadway compadres, it has its own gentle, unassuming power.
Linney and Hecht’s confident, vulnerable-lite performances are the reasons to come, and the two stage veterans embrace the audience with their affable warmth and charm.
Mr. Auburn may not have written the next great American play, but what he and his talented collaborators have provided is definitely worth the 90 minutes it takes to engage with it.
That said, it’s not quite enough to make Auburn’s play a Summer to remember.
And so was I happy for a time, to bask in the company of these two phenomenally persuasive and appealing actresses.
Summer, 1976 comes off as a literary exercise, an enacted short story about a series of situational connections with others that happen to most of us most of the time.

Opposites attract – and not only when it comes to romance, but friendships as well. That’s the thesis of Summer, 1976, a pleasant wisp of a play with an A-list pedigree that has all the dramatic heft of catching a few rays.
Except without the liquid lubrication, it comes across as fairly dry.
While brilliantly acted by Laura Linney and Jessica Hecht (both of them smartly costumed by Linda Cho), the 90-minute play ultimately feels like a stretched-out anecdote.
But at present, it feels like a star vehicle hastily slapped together, promising much and delivering little.
Under Daniel Sullivan’s sure-handed direction, they offer a marvelous masterclass in acting (on John Lee Beatty’s ingenious set).
It was a delight to experience the result of all of their work.
Together with playwright Auborn, they craft a portrait of friendship that is etched in authentic engagement and sharp insight into the characters of these two very different women.

cn.t: Linney and Hecht elevate Auburn's quietly affecting but slight two-hander about a fleeting friendship, with critics praising the stellar performances while finding the play itself pleasant but dramatically inert.

vs.sum: The Samuel J. Friedman Theatre offers good sightlines with minimal obstructions and a well-raked mezzanine, ensuring a clear view from most seats. The sound quality is consistently praised, and the seating is comfortable with decent legroom. The theater's ambiance is enhanced by its elegant design following renovation, though facilities like restrooms are average, leading to some congestion during intermissions.

acc.note: Elevator to all levels. Built-in induction loop for t-coil hearing aids.

vr.q: This play is simple but engaging and really well performed.
